85.title: The ten plagues (Exodus 7–10)
85.hook: blood, frogs, lice, swarms, pestilence, boils, hail, locusts, darkness
85.carry: ten ways to say let go
85.howItsDone: At the Passover seder, as the ten plagues are read, many Jews remove a drop of wine from their cup for each one, and recite Rabbi Judah's three-word memory code.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let my people go: the first demand, and the bricks got harder to make. Your line was it gets harder first. Did you try something a second time? Day eighty-five.

If you've been to a Passover seder, you know the moment. Someone reads out a list, and at each word, everyone at the table dips a finger in their wine and drops a drop onto their plate. Blood. Frogs. Lice. Wild beasts. Pestilence. Boils. Hail. Locusts. Darkness. The death of the firstborn. Ten drops. Little kids love it; there are even toy frogs in some homes. And then someone reads a strange line: Rabbi Judah used to make them into a code, three nonsense words from their first letters, detzach, adash, be'achav, so he could remember them. Today: the plagues, and what they're for.
screen: `TEN DROPS OF WINE.` → `BLOOD, FROGS, LICE…` → `DETZACH, ADASH, BE'ACHAV.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word is makot. Blows. Strikes. The Torah also calls them signs and wonders. And they come in a rhythm. Moses warns Pharaoh; Pharaoh refuses; the blow falls; Pharaoh begs, promises, and when it lifts, changes his mind. Again and again. They start with the Nile. The river was Egypt's life, honored as sacred, the river where Hebrew babies were thrown. It turns to blood. Then frogs come up out of it, into bedrooms and ovens and kneading bowls. Then lice from the dust. At the third plague, Pharaoh's own magicians, who copied the first two, give up. They say: "This is the finger of God." Then swarms of wild creatures, and here something new begins. The Torah says the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, was set apart; the plague didn't touch it. Then pestilence on the livestock, boils, a hail with fire running through it, locusts that eat everything the hail left. And then darkness, so thick that "they saw not one another" for three days. But the Israelites, the text says, had light where they lived. Why so many? The Torah gives an answer: God says, "against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments." The Nile, the sun, the land: things Egypt treated as divine are shown to be no match. The rabbis added another reading: every plague was a chance for Pharaoh to change. Ten warnings. Ten times the same message, louder each time. Let them go.
screen: `MAKOT: BLOWS, STRIKES.` · `THE NILE FIRST.` · `THIS IS THE FINGER OF GOD.` · `DARKNESS, BUT LIGHT IN GOSHEN.` · then, large: `TEN WAYS TO SAY LET GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing that holds people captive today. Settle, and breathe. The seder says every generation should see itself as if it had gone out of Egypt. So look around. What holds people in their own narrow place now? Debt. Addiction. Loneliness. Injustice. Fear. A phone that won't let go. Name one, for someone else or for yourself. You don't have to fix it. Just see it clearly, the way you'd see a plague. The bell holds the time.
Makot. Blows, strikes, plagues. The ten blows on Egypt, each one saying the same thing: let my people go.
Your line: ten ways to say let go. Today, notice one thing that keeps warning you, over and over, and listen before it gets louder. Day eighty-five.

86.title: Pharaoh's hard heart (Exodus 8–10)
86.hook: each time he relents, then hardens; the rabbis say a heart can harden by habit
86.howItsDone: Jewish tradition uses Pharaoh's hardening to teach about teshuvah, turning back, and about how small repeated choices shape character; Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, makot: ten blows, each one a warning. Your line was ten ways to say let go. Today, the question everyone asks about those plagues: why didn't Pharaoh just listen? Day eighty-six.

You probably know someone who can't back down. Maybe it's you. The argument is lost, everyone can see it, and still: no. Or the promise to change, made in the middle of a crisis, that disappears the moment things calm down. Frogs are everywhere, in Pharaoh's bed, in his ovens. He calls Moses in a panic: pray for me, take them away, and I'll let the people go. Moses prays, the frogs die. And the text says: when Pharaoh saw there was relief, he hardened his heart. Today: how a heart gets hard.
screen: `THE PROMISE MADE IN A CRISIS.` → `PRAY FOR ME, I'LL LET THEM GO.` → `RELIEF, AND A HARD HEART.`

segments.voice: Read the plagues closely and you'll notice a pattern in the language. In the early plagues, the Torah says Pharaoh's heart was hardened, or Pharaoh hardened his heart. It's his own doing. After the blood: "And Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them." After the frogs, the lice, the swarms, the pestilence: the same, again and again. Then, at the sixth plague, the boils, the language turns: "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh." From then on, it's mostly God who hardens it. That's troubling. If God hardened his heart, was Pharaoh still choosing? The rabbis argued about it, and they gave different answers. Maimonides said Pharaoh sinned freely at first, so badly and so often that he lost the path back. The door of turning closed, as a consequence of his own choices. Sforno, another medieval commentator, said the opposite in a way: God strengthened Pharaoh's heart so he could choose freely, and not just give in because of the pain. Either way, notice the first five times. No one forced him. And Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, has a line that fits: one wrong deed drags another after it. Every time he said no, the next no came easier. Hebrew uses three words for this hardening. One is chazak, strong, the same word as chazak at the end of Genesis. One is kaved, heavy. One is kasheh, hard. A heart can get strong in the wrong way, heavy, stiff. The rabbis' lesson is simple and a little scary: hearts harden by habit.
screen: `PHARAOH HARDENED HIS HEART.` · `AT THE BOILS: GOD HARDENED IT.` · `MAIMONIDES AND SFORNO DIFFER.` · `ONE WRONG DRAGS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `HEARTS HARDEN BY HABIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften one stance held too long. Settle, and breathe. Think of a position you've taken, with a person or an idea, that you keep repeating mostly because you've always said it. A grudge. An I'll never. An old argument with a family member. Put your hand on your chest if you like. Ask: is this still true, or just a habit? You don't have to give it up. Just loosen your grip a little. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's hard heart. He promises, then hardens, again and again, until the hardening becomes who he is.
Your line: hearts harden by habit. Today, catch yourself saying an old no, and try, once, a softer answer. Day eighty-six.

87.title: The night of the firstborn (Exodus 11–12)
87.hook: blood on the doorposts, and the Lord passes over the houses
87.tomorrow: bread with no time to rise
87.howItsDone: Every spring Jews hold a Passover seder at home, retelling the Exodus from the Haggadah; a child asks why this night is different, and the family eats matzah and bitter herbs and tells the story in answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's hard heart: every promise forgotten the moment relief came. Your line was hearts harden by habit. Did you soften one old no? Now, the last plague, and the night that became a holiday. Day eighty-seven.

Every spring, at a table full of family, the youngest child who can read stands up, sometimes nervous, sometimes showing off, and sings a question. Ma nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot? Why is this night different from all other nights? Why the flat bread? Why the bitter herbs? Why do we dip, and lean? And the whole long evening that follows is the answer. It's called the seder, and it retells one night. Today: the night of the firstborn, the night the Torah calls Pesach.
screen: `THE YOUNGEST CHILD STANDS UP.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE WHOLE EVENING IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Moses warns Pharaoh of one final blow: at midnight, every firstborn in Egypt will die. Then God gives the Israelites instructions, and they're very specific. Each household takes a lamb. On the fourteenth day of the month, they slaughter it, and put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door, with a bunch of hyssop. They roast it and eat it that night, with flat bread and bitter herbs, dressed for travel, shoes on, staff in hand, in a hurry. And no one is to go out of the house until morning. God says: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." That's Pesach. From a Hebrew root that means to pass over, or, some say, to hover over, protecting. At midnight it happens. There's a great cry in Egypt, the text says, for there was not a house where there was not one dead. It's a terrible night. The Torah doesn't hide it, and Jews have never pretended it was simple; we'll come to the spilled wine and the silenced angels later this week. And in the middle of the story, before anyone has even left, God tells them to make this night a memorial forever. It'll be retold. And the Torah says your children will ask: "What mean ye by this service?" And the commandment is: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day." That's why a child asks the questions at the seder. Freedom isn't only something that happened. It's something you tell, out loud, to the next person, every year.
screen: `A LAMB, BLOOD ON THE DOORPOSTS.` · `PESACH: TO PASS OVER.` · `A GREAT CRY IN EGYPT.` · `AND THOU SHALT TELL THY SON.` · then, large: `THIS NIGHT IS DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one thing slowly and remember. If you have something small nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, some fruit, take it. If not, just imagine it. Hold it for a moment before you eat. Think of something you were brought out of: a hard time, a narrow place, something that once held you. Then eat it slowly. Taste it. Let it be a small memorial. The bell holds the time.
Pesach. Passover. The night God passed over the marked houses, and the name of the holiday that retells it every spring.
Your line: this night is different. Tonight, do one small thing differently to remember something you're grateful to be free of. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: Bread with no time to rise (Exodus 12:33–42)
88.hook: dough on their shoulders, and a mixed multitude going with them
88.howItsDone: During the week of Passover Jews eat matzah and remove leavened bread, chametz, from their homes; at the seder the matzah is lifted and called the bread of affliction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesach: blood on the doorposts, a terrible midnight, and a child's question every spring. Your line was this night is different. Now it's morning, and it's time to go. Day eighty-eight.

You know the feeling of leaving in a rush. The taxi's downstairs. The flight is in two hours. You're grabbing half-packed bags, leaving dishes in the sink, the bread you meant to bake still sitting in a bowl. After four hundred years, it happens to a whole people in one morning. Pharaoh, broken, calls Moses and Aaron in the night: get out, all of you, go. The Egyptians push them to hurry. And the dough for tomorrow's bread hasn't risen yet. Today: the bread that didn't have time.
screen: `THE TAXI'S DOWNSTAIRS.` → `GET OUT, ALL OF YOU.` → `THE DOUGH HASN'T RISEN.`

segments.voice: The Torah paints it in one detail: "And the people took their dough before it was leavened," their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks, on their shoulders. When they stop to eat, they bake the dough into flat cakes, because they "could not tarry." That's matzah. Flour and water, baked before it can rise. And every year at Passover, Jews eat it, and remove all leavened bread from their homes for the whole week. Here's what's interesting: matzah means two opposite things at once. At the start of the seder, people lift it up and call it the bread of affliction, a phrase from Deuteronomy: the poor bread that slaves ate. And by the end of the evening it's the bread of freedom, baked in the hurry of leaving. Same bread. It depends on which side of the door you're on. Then another small detail that's easy to miss: "And a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only the children of Israel. Others came too: Egyptians, maybe other slaves, people who had seen what happened and decided to go. The Torah doesn't explain who, and it doesn't turn them away. And the text counts the time: four hundred and thirty years, and on that very day, they went out. It calls that night a night of watching, kept by God, and kept by the people ever after. When the moment came, they didn't wait for the bread to be perfect. They went.
screen: `DOUGH BEFORE IT WAS LEAVENED.` · `THE BREAD OF AFFLICTION.` · `THE BREAD OF FREEDOM.` · `A MIXED MULTITUDE WENT TOO.` · then, large: `GO WHEN IT'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one thing unfinished on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been holding back on until it's perfect. A message you keep rewriting. A plan you keep refining. A step you're waiting to feel ready for. Ask yourself: is it ready enough? Flat bread still feeds people. Decide on one thing you'll let go of as it is, today. The bell holds the time.
Matzah. Flat bread, baked before it could rise. The bread of affliction, and the bread of freedom.
Your line: go when it's time. Today, send the thing you keep polishing. Let it be flat bread. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: At the sea (Exodus 14)
89.hook: the army behind, water ahead; midrash says Nachshon walked in first
89.howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover, the day tradition says it happened, and on the Shabbat of the Song; Nachshon's story is a favorite in Jewish teaching about courage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matzah: dough on their shoulders, a mixed multitude, and no time to wait. Your line was go when it's time. Did you send the flat bread? Now they're out, and trapped. Day eighty-nine.

Freedom lasts about three days before Pharaoh changes his mind. Again. He gets his chariots, six hundred of the best, and chases them. And the Israelites are camped by the sea. They look up and see the Egyptian army coming. Water in front. Soldiers behind. Nowhere to go. And the people panic, and turn on Moses with one of the most bitter lines in the Torah: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?" Today: the moment between the army and the sea.
screen: `SIX HUNDRED CHARIOTS.` → `WATER AHEAD, SOLDIERS BEHIND.` → `WERE THERE NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?`

segments.voice: Moses answers with calm, famous words: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." Stand still. It sounds perfect. And then God says something surprising back to Moses: "Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Why are you crying out to me? Tell them to move. Go forward. Into the water? The Torah goes on: Moses lifts his staff, a strong east wind blows all night, the sea splits, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left." But the rabbis noticed a gap between go forward and the sea splitting. Who moved first? The Talmud tells a story. The tribes stood at the edge, each saying: I'm not going in first. You go. And then one man, Nachshon, son of Amminadav, a prince of the tribe of Judah, walked into the sea. Up to his ankles. His knees. His waist. His neck. The midrash says the water reached his nostrils, and only then did the sea split. There's another opinion in the same passage, that the tribe of Benjamin jumped in first. The Torah itself names no one. But the story of Nachshon stuck, so much that in modern Hebrew a nachshon is someone who goes first, a pioneer. The sea splits. The Israelites walk through on dry ground. The Egyptians follow, and the waters come back over them. The Torah says the people saw, and they believed. But first somebody had to get their feet wet.
screen: `STAND STILL, AND SEE.` · `SPEAK TO THEM, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.` · `NACHSHON WALKS IN.` · `A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.` · then, large: `WALK IN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the first step before it's easy. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're standing at the edge of. A hard conversation, an application, a doctor's appointment, a new start. Notice that part of you is waiting for the sea to split first. For the fear to go, for a sign, for someone else to go. Now imagine the first step, just ankle deep. What is it, exactly? Picture yourself taking it. The bell holds the time.
At the sea. Trapped between an army and the water, the people are told go forward, and the midrash says Nachshon walked in first.
Your line: walk in first. Today, take the first small step into the thing you've been standing at the edge of. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1–18)
90.hook: the people sing; the rabbis say God hushed the angels because the Egyptians were drowning (Megillah 10b)
90.howItsDone: Jews say the Song of the Sea in the morning prayers, and its line mi chamocha in the evening and morning prayers; at the seder many spill a drop of wine for each plague, and the Song is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the sea: an army behind, water ahead, and Nachshon walking in up to his nose. Your line was walk in first. Did you take a first step? Now they're on the other side. Day ninety.

Think of the biggest relief you've ever felt. The test result that came back clear. The phone call saying they're safe. The moment you realize the thing chasing you is gone. Now multiply it by a whole people, standing on a beach at dawn, soaking wet, looking back at the water where the army was. Generations of slavery, and it's over. What do you do in a moment like that? They sing. Today: the song, and the angels who weren't allowed to join in.
screen: `THE BIGGEST RELIEF YOU'VE FELT.` → `A PEOPLE ON A BEACH AT DAWN.` → `THEY SING.`

segments.voice: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD." And the song begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea." It's called Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, which many scholars count among the oldest poems in the Bible. In a Torah scroll it's even written differently from the text around it, laid out in a pattern like bricks in a wall. And one line from it, "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?" in Hebrew mi chamocha, is said in Jewish prayer every single day. So the song is honored. Nobody tells the people they were wrong to sing. But the Talmud tells a story about that same moment. Up in heaven, it says, the ministering angels wanted to sing too. And God stopped them. The works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you want to sing? The Egyptians were enemies. They'd enslaved and chased the Israelites. And they were still God's creatures. The Talmud adds a subtle line: God doesn't rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, though God may let others rejoice. The people who were just saved can sing. But nobody should throw a party over someone drowning. In the same spirit, at the seder, when the ten plagues are read, many people spill a drop of wine for each one. A full cup is a sign of joy, and the joy is made a little less, because people suffered. The book of Proverbs says it too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." You can be grateful you're safe. You can sing. Just don't sing over the drowning.
screen: `I WILL SING UNTO THE LORD.` · `MI CHAMOCHA, EVERY DAY.` · `GOD HUSHES THE ANGELS.` · `A DROP OF WINE FOR EACH PLAGUE.` · then, large: `REJOICE NOT WHEN THINE ENEMY FALLETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: celebrate without gloating. Settle, and breathe. Think of a recent win. Something that went your way: an argument you won, a game, a promotion, a rival who stumbled. Let yourself be glad about it. Really glad. Then think of the person on the other side. What did it cost them? Hold both at once, the joy and the other person. If you pray, you can give thanks for what went well. The bell holds the time.
The Song of the Sea. Shirat HaYam. The people's song of thanks on the far shore, sung while the angels were told to be quiet.
screen: `THE SONG OF THE SEA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: don't sing over the drowning. Today, when something goes your way, enjoy it, and be kind to whoever it didn't go well for. Day ninety.

91.title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
91.hook: the prophetess takes a drum and leads the women in dance
91.howItsDone: Miriam's song is read in synagogue with the Song of the Sea each year, and in many communities women mark it by singing and drumming together, some on the seventh day of Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of the Sea, and God hushing the angels. Your line was don't sing over the drowning. It's the end of a week: the plagues, a hard heart, the night of the firstborn, bread with no time to rise, the sea, the song. Day ninety-one.

Think about the last time you had to leave a place in a hurry. A fire alarm, a flight you nearly missed, a move that happened too fast. You grab what matters: keys, phone, the kids, maybe a photo. Now picture the night the Israelites left Egypt. They left so fast the bread didn't have time to rise. And yet, on the far shore of the sea, when the water has closed and the people are safe, one woman reaches into her bag and pulls out a drum. And then another woman does. And another. Somebody packed the drums. Today: Miriam, and the drum she brought.

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." Three things in that one line. First, the title. Miriam is called a prophetess, the first woman in the Torah given that name. The rabbis ask why she's called the sister of Aaron and not of Moses, and the Talmud answers with a story: she was prophesying when she was only Aaron's sister, before Moses was even born, that her mother would have a son who would save the people. She's the girl who watched the basket on the Nile. Now she's leading a nation. Second, the drum. A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame with skin stretched over it, the kind you hold up and strike with your palm. And here's the question the midrash asks: where did these women get drums, in the desert, after leaving in such a rush? The answer, repeated by the great commentator Rashi, is that the women were so sure God would do wonders for them that they packed their drums in Egypt. They carried the celebration before there was anything to celebrate. Third, the song. Miriam sings a single line back to the women, "Sing ye to the LORD, for He is highly exalted", the same line Moses opened with. Moses sings the long song. Miriam gets everyone dancing. Both belong to the story. Many Jewish women today point to this verse when they sing, drum and lead in their own communities. And the lesson inside it is quiet and practical. Hope isn't only a feeling. Sometimes it's a thing you put in your bag.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move for one minute. If you can stand, stand. If you can't, your hands and shoulders will do. Tap a rhythm on your leg or the table, like a hand drum. Sway. Nod. Nobody is watching, and nobody is grading. Let the body say something the mouth doesn't need to. Then, for the second minute, be still, and notice your heartbeat, the drum you always carry. The bell holds the time.
Miriam's timbrel. A hand drum, carried out of Egypt by women who were sure they'd need it, and played on the far shore of the sea.
Your line: bring the drum. Today, bring one thing that makes joy easier to wherever you're going: a song, a snack to share, a good word. Pack it before you need it. Day ninety-one.
